A pipe that carries coal slurry from the Kanawha Eagle Prep Plant in Kanawha County to an adjacent settling pond burst, causing the spill. It was reported to the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) by the company at 7:30 a.m., and later that day began to reach the Kanawha River, some 3.5 miles away from the site of the spill.

Coal slurry or sludge is a waste fluid produced by washing coal with water and chemicals prior to shipping the coal to market. When coal is mined underground or by highwall or auger miners, there are significant amounts of rocks and clays mixed in. This is a guide that I hope will help users if they have a problem with their filesystem.

You may never have this problem, but I recently used dd (a low-level copying and file conversion command) to clone a hard drive a couple of times and ended up messing up my main hard drive somehow. I've fixed it, and I thought I'd share how to do it here.

So your system won't boot and gives a "bad superblock" error. If you get a prompt while booting, you should try to run fsck manually in that prompt. (For the purposes of this post, I'm assuming you're using an ext4 file system. If you're not, change ext4 to the type you're using.)

That'll likely give you more info.

Next, get a live USB/CD/DVD with a Linux distro on it. It doesn't really matter what type. I happened to have a GParted Live USB lying around, so I used that. Boot into it.

Now, open a terminal. We want to see where your partitions are. Run (where root# indicates you need to run the command with sudo or as the root user):

root# fdisk -l

The output should look something like this (make sure that the partitions aren't mounted):

NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT
Disk /dev/sda: 232.9 GiB, 250059350016 bytes, 488397168 sectors
Units: sectors of 1 * 512 = 512 bytes
Sector size (logical/physical): 512 bytes / 512 bytes
I/O size (minimum/optimal): 512 bytes / 512 bytes
Disklabel type: dos
Disk identifier: 0x88baf3d9

Device Boot Start End Sectors Size Id Type
/dev/sda1 * 2048 52430847 52428800 25G 83 Linux
/dev/sda2 52430848 480008191 427577344 203.9G 83 Linux
/dev/sda3 480008192 488396799 8388608 4G 82 Linux swap / Solaris

This is the output from a system that is booted into its main hard drive. In your case, your partitions shouldn't have mountpoints in a live boot. Now, you'll need to make sure you're working on the right partition. In this case, I may have problems with sda1 or sda2.

To check and fix these, I'll run:

root# fsck.ext4 -v /dev/sda1

root# fsck.ext4 -v /dev/sda2

Let it fix what problems it finds and reboot into your main system. That should resolve the issue.
